description:
Our team brings together different interests, perspectives, and skills, with a shared passion for technology, education, research, and problem-solving. We value collaboration, creativity, critical thinking, and taking initiative.

As a team, we are interested in exploring new approaches, learning from one another, and challenging ourselves through this experience. Our strengths include communication, research, project coordination, analytical thinking, and creative problem-solving.
summary: Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a free, browser-based tool that answers one question for any point on the Moon and any date: will a lander have sunlight and a line of sight to Earth? It combines NASA LOLA terrain with JPL Horizons-validated ephemerides to show when the Sun and Earth rise above the real local horizon, how much solar power a lander can generate, how long it must survive on batteries, and how relay satellites fill communication gaps. A landing date planner ranks the best days, and scenario comparison lets planners test backup plans side by side. This matters because near the lunar south pole the Sun skims the horizon, so a few days or a few hundred metres can decide whether a mission survives. A Learn mode explains every number, so students and mission planners use the same tool.
details:
The user picks a landing site (a curated site, a click on the map, or custom coordinates) and a landing date and time. The app then computes:

- the Sun's and Earth's elevation above the terrain horizon, drawn as a 360° panorama;

- a 30-day timeline of when each is visible, with day-start and contact-loss countdowns;

- direct-to-Earth contact versus contact through relays (NRHO, ELFO, L2 halo);

- solar power and battery size for a user-defined panel area, efficiency, mounting and load;

- a landing date planner, a 3 km-spaced 9×9 scan of the surroundings, and a scenario comparison.

Sun and Earth positions come from an in-browser model (astronomy-engine plus the IAU lunar rotation model with libration). It agrees with JPL Horizons (DE441) to within 0.004° (RMS 0.001°), and 18 curated sites use pre-downloaded Horizons data for Nov 2026–Dec 2027. Horizon profiles are ray-traced through LOLA digital elevation models to 300 km from an observer 2 m above ground.

Benefits:It turns a multi-tool, expert-only analysis into one page that works on any device with no installation, and it shows how sensitive a mission is to its landing date and exact position. Results can be shared as links and exported as CSV or PDF.

Intended impact: Faster early-stage trade studies for mission planners, a teaching tool for students and educators, and a clearer public understanding of why the lunar south pole is both valuable and difficult. The Learn mode and guided tour serve beginners, and the Expert mode serves professionals.

Tools and technologies: NASA LOLA elevation data, JPL Horizons ephemerides (DE441), astronomy-engine, an IAU lunar orientation model, hosted on GitHub Pages with open source code on GitHub.

Creativity:

- It is built around the real horizon, so you see what a lander would see, not just a sun-angle number.

- It connects the numbers to decisions: battery mass, best landing day, relay need.

- Every section explains itself, with plain-language "why this matters" notes and reality checks (for example, comparing the Moon with Earth).

Factors considered.

- Accuracy versus accessibility:Quick mode runs instantly in the browser (3.8 km terrain, about 0.1–1° accuracy), and Precise mode, a downloadable version, uses full 80 m NASA maps.

- Honest limits: the app states its resolution, data sources and the lack of atmosphere or refraction, and NASA publishes no centre points for Artemis III regions.

- Two audiences:a shared engine serves students and professionals.

- Reliability: results are checked against Horizons.
